T1: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing-protection products for specific use cases because they value specialized performance and aesthetics for those activities. Who benefits: End‑users (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, outdoor enthusiasts) gain better hearing protection tailored to their unique needs.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is designed to meet specific activity demands (e.g., sound transmission for concerts, noise reduction for industrial work, comfort for outdoor activities), users are willing to pay a premium and adopt dedicated devices.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering distinct product lines (e.g., musician headphones, industrial earmuffs) at premium prices, leveraging its existing R&D and brand reputation, and potentially expanding direct‑to‑consumer sales.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for specialized hearing protection.; Hellberg can design and market products differentiated for each use case.; The market for specialized hearing protection is large enough to justify a separate line.. Predictions: Surveyed users will express higher intent to purchase a specialized product compared to a generic hearing protector.; Sales of Hellberg products in targeted use cases will grow faster than overall market growth..

T2: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing-protection products because they already own multiple pairs and seek to minimize hassle and cost. Who benefits: Consumers benefit by owning a single solution for multiple use cases, reducing the need to buy multiple devices.. Why behaviour changes: When a product can serve multiple activities (e.g., home, office, outdoor), users are motivated to switch to a single device to avoid owning and managing multiple pairs.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering versatile, multi‑purpose hearing protectors at competitive prices, leveraging its existing brand for multiple‑device adoption, and potentially expanding to direct‑to‑consumer channels.. Assumptions: Consumers are already owning multiple hearing devices for different activities.; A single, versatile product can be marketed effectively as a cost‑saving solution.; The market for multi‑purpose hearing protection is large enough to justify a separate line.. Predictions: Surveyed users will report owning multiple hearing devices for different uses.; Willingness to pay for a multi‑purpose device will be higher than for a generic single‑purpose product..

Test "Consumer Choice Test: Specialized vs Multi-Use Hearing Protection" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 300 adult consumers (150 per group) via a panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two product descriptions: (A) a specialized hearing protector designed for a single use case (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, hunters) with price €120; (B) a multi-use hearing protector marketed as suitable for multiple activities (home, office, outdoor) with price €100. Both descriptions include the same basic safety features and brand reputation. Participants are asked to indicate their intent to purchase (1‑10 scale) and the maximum price they would pay. The test also collects demographic data (age, occupation, previous hearing‑protection ownership).. Sample: 300 adult consumers (150 per group) recruited via an online panel to match the target demographic of Hellberg’s existing customer base.. Measure: Primary outcome: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each product description. Secondary outcome: maximum price willing to pay (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Group A (specialized product) will have a higher average purchase intent and maximum price than Group B (multi‑use product).; T2: Group B (multi‑use product) will have a higher average purchase intent and maximum price than Group A (specialized product).. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than for Group B, conclude T1 is better supported. If the average purchase intent for Group B is at least 1.5 points higher than for Group A, conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the evidence is inconclusive and the test does not resolve the theories.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Who benefits: Home‑studio creators gain superior audio quality and professional cred, and Neumann can capture premium pricing by offering a clear signal of quality.. Why behaviour changes: Creators migrate from starter kits to professional gear when they want to produce music that sounds as good as in professional studios, and they value a product that is endorsed as a pro‑level tool.. Why behaviour changes: Creators migrate from starter kits to professional gear when they need to produce audio that sounds good on multiple platforms (streaming, YouTube, podcasts), and they value a product that is endorsed for streaming quality.. How value is captured: Neumann can price the product at a premium, sell through professional audio retailers, and promote the product as a solution for streaming, generating higher margins and stronger brand equity.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay a premium for consistent audio quality across platforms.; Professional recognition is a secondary driver for streaming‑focused purchases.; There is sufficient demand within the home‑studio market for streaming‑focused products.. Predictions: Creators will show higher purchase intent for a product explicitly marketed for streaming quality.; Sales of higher‑priced models will correlate with creator self‑identification as content creators or streamers.; Retailers will report increased demand for studio mics marketed for streaming from creators..

Test "Home Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 300 home studio creators (defined as individuals who produce music, podcasts, or video content at home and use microphones). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups. Group A receives a product description emphasizing professional recognition and studio quality (e.g., "Pro‑level studio microphone for serious home studio owners"). Group B receives a product description emphasizing streaming quality and consistent audio across platforms (e.g., "Mic for professional‑grade streaming and content creation"). Both groups view the same product (e.g., Neumann TLM102) with the same price point. After viewing, participants indicate their intent to purchase on a 7‑point Likert scale (1‑“Very unlikely” to 7‑“Very likely”).. Sample: 300 home studio creators recruited via online panels, balanced for gender, age, and experience level.. Measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑7) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent than Group B because creators value professional recognition and are willing to pay a premium for it.; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent than Group A because creators need consistent audio quality across platforms and are willing to pay for it.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average intent is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B’s average intent, conclude T1 is better supported. If Group B’s average intent is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A’s average intent, conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude neither theory is strongly supported.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not expand the product line yet. Conduct the proposed Home Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test to measure whether professional recognition (T1) or streaming quality (T2) drives higher purchase intent. If the test shows a difference of at least 1.5 points, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition for the identified segment. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, maintain the current professional range.  Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not expand the product line yet. Conduct the proposed Home Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test to measure whether professional recognition (T1) or streaming quality (T2) drives higher purchase intent. If the test shows a difference of at least 1.5 points, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition for the identified segment. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, maintain the current professional range. Target customer: Home studio creators (individuals who produce music, podcasts, or video content at home and use microphones).. Value proposition: A differentiated studio microphone proposition that either emphasizes professional recognition and studio quality (T1) or consistent audio quality across platforms (T2), depending on which segment shows higher purchase intent.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Home Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test (300 creators, simulated product descriptions, 7‑point purchase intent scale) within the €15,000 budget and 6‑week timeline.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain because the available evidence does not directly address which factor (professional recognition vs. streaming quality) drives higher purchase intent among home studio creators.. Would change if: If the test shows a difference of at least 1.5 points in purchase intent between the two groups, the favoured theory would shift to the group with the higher intent.; If the test shows no difference (difference < 1.5 points), both theories would be weakened, and the recommendation would remain unchanged: maintain the current professional range.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Constraints: Limited to public sources; financial data may not be available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must be from credible sources; company claims alone are insufficient.; Any recommendation must be justified by observable demand or market signals.. T1: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it offers a clear, measurable benefit beyond basic protection (e.g., comfort, style, or specific use-case features). Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking hearing protection for specific activities (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, children) who value comfort, style, or functional features.. Why behaviour changes: When a product offers a tangible advantage that addresses their unique needs, consumers are more likely to purchase it over generic alternatives.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by pricing premium for differentiated features, leveraging brand reputation for specialized products, and potentially expanding into new consumer segments.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for features that address their specific use cases.; Differentiation is a key driver of purchase decisions for this segment.; Hellberg can effectively communicate these benefits to consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated product (e.g., musician-specific earplugs with sound filtering) versus a generic version, purchase intent or conversion rate will be higher among consumers who identify as musicians.; Surveyed consumers will rank comfort, style, or specific use-case features as top reasons for choosing a differentiated product over a generic one..

T2: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is marketed as a status or lifestyle accessory, leveraging fashion and design appeal. Who benefits: Individual consumers who value style, status, and design as primary purchase drivers for hearing protection.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is presented as a fashionable or desirable accessory, consumers are motivated to buy it for social signaling rather than purely functional reasons.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by premium pricing, limited editions, and brand collaborations, creating a differentiated product line that appeals to consumers beyond safety.. Assumptions: Fashion and design are significant purchase drivers for hearing protection among certain consumer segments.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for stylish hearing protection.; Hellberg can effectively communicate design and brand value to target consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a designer-branded hearing protector versus a generic version, purchase intent or conversion rate will be higher among consumers who rank style and status as top priorities.; Surveyed consumers will cite design aesthetics or brand prestige as primary reasons for choosing a differentiated product over a generic one..

Test "Differentiated vs Generic Hearing Protection Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 300 adult consumers (18-65) via a panel, stratified by age and self-reported hearing protection use (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, hobbyists). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a generic hearing protector (standard protection, no additional features). Group B receives the same description plus a differentiated feature (e.g., Bluetooth connectivity, customizable color, or a specific use-case benefit). Both descriptions are identical except for the differentiated feature. Participants are asked to indicate their likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale) and their maximum price they would pay. The test measures the impact of the differentiated feature on purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Sample: 300 adult consumers (18-65) recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and self-reported hearing protection use (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, hobbyists).. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Group B (differentiated feature) will have a higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A (generic feature).; T2: Group B will not have a statistically significant higher purchase intent or willingness to pay than Group A, because status/design appeal is not a primary driver for this segment.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Group B is at least 1.5 points higher than for Group A (on a 1‑10 scale), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude that the differentiated feature does not significantly drive purchase intent and abandon the proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Differentiated vs Generic Hearing Protection Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated feature versus a generic version. If the test shows a statistically significant 1.5-point higher purchase intent for the differentiated version, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, abandon the proposition and focus ‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated result SYN-B concerns comfort and wear frequency, not consumer demand for differentiated features. It does not address T1, which predicts purchase intent driven by differentiated features. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it offers a clear, measurable benefit beyond basic protection (e.g., comfort, style, or specific use-case features).. Evidence: SYN-B.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Differentiated vs Generic Hearing Protection Purchase Intent Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated feature versus a generic version. If the test shows a statistically significant 1.5-point higher purchase intent for the differentiated version, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, abandon the proposition and focus ‑ Target customer: Individual consumers (18-65) who use hearing protection for specific activities (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, hobbyists) and value comfort, style, or specific use-case features.. Value proposition: A differentiated hearing protector that offers a tangible benefit beyond basic protection (e.g., Bluetooth connectivity, customizable color, or a specific use-case benefit) to capture premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 8‑week, €15,000 test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a differentiated feature versus a generic version.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company claims and a single simulated result; actual consumer demand for differentiated features is unknown. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows a <1.5-point difference in purchase intent between differentiated and generic versions, the favoured theory would shift to neutral, and the recommendation would be to maintain the existing product portfolio.; If additional credible sources (e.g., market surveys, sales data) demonstrate strong consumer demand for differentiated features, the favoured theory would shift to likely, and the recommendation would be to invest in a differentiated line.; If a competitor successfully launches a differentiated product with measurable sales growth, the favoured theory would shift to likely, and the recommendation would be to pursue differentiation.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, and identify the key evidence that would support this decision.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; cannot use later developments.; No internal company data; must rely on external evidence.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.; Must consider the existing dealer network and individual buyer reach of Deere.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, residential lawn care, or a niche industrial application).; 2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on the existing tractor, combine, and industrial equipment markets through dealers.; 4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products (if feasible)..

T1: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are affordable, practical for small gardens, and easy to maintain, creating a market demand that Deere can capture by offering a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Small‑holder homeowners and renters who need a versatile, inexpensive tool for yard work.. Why behaviour changes: Rising home ownership and small‑garden ownership increase the number of households seeking affordable, multipurpose yard equipment.. How value is captured: Deere can sell directly to consumers through its existing dealer network, offering a lower‑margin consumer product that leverages existing distribution and brand trust.. Assumptions: Small‑garden ownership rates in the U.S. were growing in the early 1960s.; Consumers value affordability and ease of maintenance over premium features.; Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor at a price point competitive with existing brands.. Predictions: Sales of lawn and garden tractors will grow faster than tractor sales to farms and large industrial users.; Deere can capture a share of the consumer market without cannibalizing its core tractor business.; Consumer demand will be sufficient to justify a dedicated consumer line..

T2: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are a status symbol and a symbol of home ownership, creating a market demand that Deere can capture by offering a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes brand prestige. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who use lawn care as a way to signal social status and demonstrate property ownership.. Why behaviour changes: Growing suburbanization and home ownership rates in the early 1960s increase the number of households seeking products that signal affluence and community status.. How value is captured: Deere can price consumer tractors at a premium, leveraging its existing brand prestige and dealer network to command higher margins.. Assumptions: Home ownership rates in the U.S. were rising in the early 1960s.; Consumers associate lawn care with social status and community.; Deere can position its consumer line as a prestige item without cannibalizing core tractor sales.. Predictions: Sales of lawn and garden tractors will be concentrated among homeowners and renters, not primarily farmers.; Premium pricing will be acceptable to consumers who value brand prestige.; Deere can capture a segment of the market that values status over affordability..

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions: one emphasizing affordability and practicality for small gardens, and one emphasizing prestige and status. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens (under 0.5 acres) in the U.S. They are asked to indicate their primary reason for purchasing a lawn and garden tractor (e.g., affordability, status, or other).. Sample: 500 households with small gardens, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and geographic region.. Measure: Primary purchase motivation (affordability vs. status) measured on a 1‑7 Likert scale (1 = affordability, 7 = status). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) for each product variant.. Predictions: T1: Participants exposed to the affordability description will report affordability as their primary reason (average score ≥ 4) and will show higher WTP for the affordability variant.; T2: Participants exposed to the prestige description will report status as their primary reason (average score ≥ 4) and will show higher WTP for the prestige variant.. Decision rule: If the average primary motivation score for the affordability variant is at least 4 and at least 1.5 points higher than the prestige variant, T1 is supported. If the prestige variant score is at least 4 and at least 1.5 points higher, T2 is supported. If neither variant meets the threshold, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test whether affordability or prestige drives purchase decisions. If the survey shows affordability as the primary driver with a threshold of at least 4 on the 1‑7 Likert scale and a 1.5‑point advantage over prestige, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small‑ ‑ ‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivations for lawn and garden tractors. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts demand based on affordability and practicality for small gardens. New claim: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are affordable, practical for small gardens, and easy to maintain, creating a market demand that Deere can capture by offering a differentiated consumer proposition.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (X1) to test whether affordability or prestige drives purchase decisions. If the survey shows affordability as the primary driver with a threshold of at least 4 on the 1‑7 Likert scale and a 1.5‑point advantage over prestige, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small‑ ‑ ‑ Target customer: Small‑holder homeowners and renters with small gardens (under 0.5 acres) who seek affordable, practical yard equipment.. Value proposition: A lawn and garden tractor priced at a level comparable to existing competitive brands, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network to reach consumers directly.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Preference Survey (X1) within the €15,000 budget and 12‑week timeline.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to a single independent study showing a 76‑percent sales growth for lawn and garden equipment from 1960 to 1979. There is no direct evidence that consumers purchase tractors for affordability versus prestige. A . Would change if: If the survey shows prestige as the primary driver with a threshold of at least 4 and a 1.5‑point advantage over affordability, we would shift focus to a prestige‑driven proposition.; If the survey shows neither driver meets the threshold, we would remain uncertain and consider other options such as licensing or expanding the existing dealer network.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will purchase differentiated hearing protection if it is marketed as a lifestyle/fashion accessory for non‑work use (e.g., music, leisure), because they value style, comfort, and multiple‑pair ownership, allowing premium pricing. Who benefits: Consumers seeking stylish and comfortable hearing protection for recreational activities; Hellberg Safety benefits from higher margins and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: If perceived as a fashion item rather than a purely functional tool, consumers will be willing to buy multiple units and pay a premium, increasing sales.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by introducing limited‑edition designs, premium pricing, and retail partnerships to create a lifestyle brand.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with style and comfort, not just necessity.; There is sufficient market space for a fashion-focused hearing‑protection category.; Hellberg can design and market products that meet these lifestyle expectations.. Predictions: Sales of a fashion‑focused product line will exceed base hearing‑protection sales in the first year.; Consumers will report higher willingness to pay and repeat‑purchase intent compared to standard protective products..

T2: Consumers will purchase differentiated hearing protection if it is marketed as a health‑and‑wellness accessory for stress‑relief and sleep improvement, because they value wellness benefits, and they are willing to pay a premium for products that address health concerns. Who benefits: Consumers seeking wellness-focused hearing protection; Hellberg Safety benefits from premium pricing and brand extension into health‑tech market.. Test "Brand-Status vs Quality Messaging Test for Home-Studio Creators" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with random assignment to two conditions. Participants are recruited from a panel of home-studio creators (YouTubers, podcasters, etc.) via social media and creator forums. They are randomly assigned to one of two product descriptions for the same Neumann TLM102 microphone: Condition A emphasizes professional-grade quality and high-fidelity audio performance ("Neumann TLM102: Professional-Grade Microphone for Studio Quality"). Condition B emphasizes brand status and professional differentiation ("Neumann TLM102: The Choice of Top Creators for Professional Status"). Both descriptions include the same price point (e.g., €899) and basic product features. After viewing their assigned description, participants are asked the primary purchase driver ("Which factor is most important to you when choosing a studio microphone?" - Quality/Performance vs Brand Status). They also rate a . Sample: 500 home-studio creators (250 per condition). Sample is recruited to ensure diversity in experience level (beginner, intermediate, advanced) and content type (music, podcasting, video).. Measure: Primary purchase driver: binary choice (Quality/Performance vs Brand Status). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros, measured by an open-ended question: "What is the maximum amount you would pay for this microphone?". Predictions: T1: Condition A will have a higher proportion of participants selecting "Quality/Performance" as the primary purchase driver and will report a higher WTP than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will have a higher proportion of participants selecting "Brand Status" as the primary purchase driver and will report a higher WTP than Condition A.. Decision rule: If the proportion of participants selecting "Quality/Performance" in Condition A exceeds the proportion in Condition B by at least 10 percentage points (p < 0.05) AND the average WTP in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least €100, then T1 is supported. If the opposite is true, then T2 is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer willingness-to-pay survey for home body-fat analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 300 respondents (150 health-conscious, 150 privacy-conscious) from a panel. Randomly assign each respondent to one of two price points: €120 (low) or €180 (high). Ask: "Would you purchase a home body-fat analyser at this price?" (binary yes/no). Also collect demographic data (age, gender, income).. Sample: 300 respondents (150 per segment). Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage saying yes to the price offer). Secondary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each segment.. Predictions: T1: Health-conscious segment will have a purchase intent rate ≥15% at €120 and ≥20% at €180; privacy-conscious segment will have a purchase intent rate ≤10% at both prices.; T2: Privacy-conscious segment will have a purchase intent rate ≥15% at €120 and ≥20% at €180; health-conscious segment will have a purchase intent rate ≤10% at both prices.. Decision rule: If health-conscious segment purchase intent at €120 ≥15% and privacy-conscious segment purchase intent at €120 ≤10%, conclude T1 is better supported. If privacy-conscious segment purchase intent at €120 ≥15% and health-conscious segment purchase intent at €120 ≤10%, conclude T2 is better supported. If neither segment meets the threshold, conclude neither theory is supported.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Brand vs. Price Sensitivity Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two randomized groups. Group A receives a product description emphasizing Neumann’s professional-grade audio performance and brand prestige. Group B receives the same description but with price emphasis (e.g., €1,200 price point). Both groups are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale (1‑€2,000) and their primary purchase driver (quality vs. price).. Sample: 500 home-studio creators recruited via social media and creator forums, balanced for experience level (beginner‑“”“”“”“”).. Measure: Average WTP and the proportion of participants selecting “quality” as the primary purchase driver.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average WTP and a higher proportion selecting “quality” as primary driver.; T2: Group B will have a higher average WTP and a higher proportion selecting “price” as primary driver.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average WTP is at least €1,500 higher than Group B’s, and the proportion selecting “quality” is at least 10 percentage points higher, conclude T1 is better supported. If Group B’s average WTP is at least €1,500 higher and the proportion selecting “price” is at least 10 percentage points higher, conclude T2 is better supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Recruit 500 adults (250 women, 250 men) aged 18-45 from the United States and Europe via a panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: (1) "Fashion Focus" condition receives a description of a hearing protection product emphasizing aesthetic design, comfort, and status signaling; (2) "Safety Focus" condition receives a description of the same product emphasizing safety features, compliance, and industrial/construction use. Both descriptions include price at €89. After reading the description, participants are asked: "How likely are you to purchase this hearing protection?" (1=Very unlikely, 5=Very likely) and "How much would you be willing to pay?" (open amount).. Sample: 500 adults (250 women, 250 men) recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, region, and income.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent (likelihood to buy on a 1‑5 scale). 2) Maximum price willingness to pay (open amount).. Predictions: T1: In the Fashion Focus condition, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than in the Safety Focus condition, and the average willingness to pay will be at least €10 higher.; T2: In the Safety Focus condition, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than in the Fashion Focus condition, and the average willingness to pay will be at least €10 higher.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 15 percentage points (e.g., Fashion Focus at 4.5, Safety Focus at 3), the evidence supports the theory that fashion messaging drives demand. If the difference is less than 15 points, the evidence does not support either theory.. Cost: 12000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case because they seek specialized protection tailored to their activity, and Hellberg can capture value by offering a product that matches their needs, allowing premium pricing and brand loyalty. Who benefits: Consumers gain protection that is optimized for their specific activity (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, construction). Hellberg benefits from higher margins and brand differentiation.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are willing to pay more for products that address their unique safety needs, and Hellberg can differentiate its brand by offering specialized solutions.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price the differentiated product at a premium, capture higher margins, and build brand loyalty among consumers who value specialized protection.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for specialized hearing protection.; Hellberg can design and manufacture a product that meets the specific needs of the target use case.; Distribution channels can be adapted to reach the target consumer segment.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated product for a specific use case, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic hearing protector.; Willingness to pay will be at least 15% higher for the differentiated product compared to a standard model..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case because they seek a product that is marketed as a lifestyle accessory or status symbol, and Hellberg can capture value by branding the product as a premium, fashion-forward item, allowing higher margins and brand extension. Who benefits: Consumers gain a product that signals status and style, and Hellberg benefits from premium pricing and brand extension into lifestyle markets.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are willing to pay more for products that convey status and are marketed as fashion items, and Hellberg can differentiate its brand by emphasizing design and style.. How value is captured: Hellberg can price the differentiated product at a premium, capture higher margins, and build brand loyalty among consumers who value status and design.. Assumptions: Consumers associate hearing protection with status and style.; Hellberg can design a product that is aesthetically appealing and marketed as a lifestyle accessory.; Distribution channels can be adapted to reach fashion-conscious consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated product marketed as a fashion accessory, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic hearing protector.; Willingness to pay will be at least 10% higher for the differentiated product compared to a standard model..

Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, construction) marketed as a specialized solution; (2) a differentiated consumer proposition marketed as a fashion accessory or lifestyle item. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults who have purchased hearing protection in the past 12 months. They are randomly assigned to view one concept first, then the other, and asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 500 participants (250 per concept) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and prior hearing‑protection purchase.. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher for the specialized concept than for the lifestyle concept, because consumers seek specialized protection and are willing to pay a premium.; T2: Purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher for the lifestyle concept than for the specialized concept, because consumers seek status and design and are willing to pay a premium for a fashion accessory.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the specialized concept is at least 15 percentage points higher than for the lifestyle concept, we conclude that T1 is better supported. If the lifestyle concept is at least 15 percentage points higher, we conclude that T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, we cannot conclude either theory.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

If the test shows a ≥15‑point difference in favor of the specialized Target customer: Consumers who purchase hearing protection for specific activities (e.g., musicians, industrial workers, construction) and value specialized protection.. Value proposition: A differentiated hearing protector that matches the user’s activity needs, offering superior performance and brand differentiation, allowing premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €20,000 budget, using the proposed method and sample.. Test "Differentiated vs Generic Hearing Protection Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 300 consumers (150 per segment) via a panel, stratified by age (18‑35 and 36‑55) and self‑identified interest in fashion/style. Participants are shown a generic hearing protector (standard safety features) and a differentiated version (same safety features plus Bluetooth connectivity, stylish design, and limited‑edition branding). They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. The test is run over 12 weeks, with results analyzed by segment.. Sample: 300 consumers (150 per segment) recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and fashion interest.. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the differentiated version will be at least 15% higher than for the generic version among both age segments.; T2: Purchase intent for the differentiated version will be at least 15% higher than for the generic version among participants who rank style/fashion as a top purchase criterion, while the difference will be smaller or non‑existent among participants who rank safety/functionality as top criterion.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the differentiated version exceeds the generic version by at least 15 percentage points in both age segments, we conclude T1 is supported. If the difference is only significant among style‑focused participants, we conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, we conclude neither theory is supported.. Cost: 15000 euros, 12 weeks.

case.question: It is mid-1962. Should Deere & Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its tractor engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Because of this, many John Deere dealers were selling some of these lines or other brands of lawn and garden tractors because Deere didn’t offer any.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.

Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; cannot use later developments.; No internal company data; must rely on external evidence.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.; Must consider the existing dealer network and individual buyer reach of Deere.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, residential lawn care, or a niche industrial application).; 2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on the existing tractor, combine, and industrial equipment markets through dealers.; 4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products (if feasible)..

T1: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they need a reliable, durable machine for routine yard work, and Deere can capture value by offering a high‑quality product through its existing dealer network. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and small‑holder farmers who need a functional, long‑lasting tractor for lawn and garden tasks.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently rely on generic lawn mowers or other brands; they will switch to Deere if they perceive Deere as a trusted, durable brand that is readily available through existing dealers.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors directly to dealers, who then sell to consumers, earning a margin on each unit and building brand loyalty that can support future sales.. Assumptions: Deere’s existing dealer network can reach individual buyers effectively.; Consumers value durability and reliability over price.; Deere can produce tractors at a cost that allows a dealer margin.. Predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn and garden tractor, dealers will report increased sales of that model compared to other brands.; Consumer surveys will show higher brand trust for Deere among lawn and garden tractor owners.; Deere’s market share in lawn and garden tractors will increase in regions where dealers are active..

T2: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are willing to pay a premium for a brand that offers a superior user experience, and Deere can capture value by positioning its tractors as premium, high‑quality products sold through dealers. Who benefits: Individual homeowners who value style, performance, and brand prestige, and are willing to pay more for a premium product.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently purchase generic or low‑cost tractors; they will switch to Deere if they perceive Deere as a status‑symbol and are willing to pay a premium for a superior experience.. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors at a premium price through dealers, who can justify the higher cost by highlighting brand prestige and performance, earning higher margins and fostering brand loyalty.. Assumptions: Consumers associate Deere with quality and status.; Deere can produce tractors that meet or exceed perceived premium standards.; Dealers can communicate premium positioning effectively to consumers.. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking distinctive, comfortable hearing protection that reflects their identity or lifestyle.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is marketed as a fashion accessory or activity-specific solution, consumers are willing to pay more for a product that signals their values and interests.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering limited-edition designs, personalization options, and higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales, leveraging its design expertise to create a differentiated brand.. T2: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is marketed as a safety-first product that complies with stringent regulations, creating demand for high-quality, reliable protection that is perceived as a professional choice. Why behaviour changes: When a product is positioned as a regulatory-grade solution, consumers trust it as a safe choice, and industrial buyers prioritize compliance, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for certified products.. Predictions: Surveyed industrial buyers will indicate willingness to pay at least 10% more for a hearing protector with a visible compliance certification.; Sales of compliance-focused products will show higher unit margins compared to standard product lines.; Compliance-focused marketing will generate higher lead conversion rates among safety-focused segments..

T1: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it offers a unique, customizable experience that aligns with personal style or activity, creating demand for premium pricing. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking distinctive, comfortable hearing protection that reflects their identity or lifestyle.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is marketed as a fashion accessory or activity-specific solution, consumers are willing to pay more for a product that signals their values and interests.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by offering limited-edition designs, personalization options, and higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales, leveraging its design expertise to create a differentiated brand.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for hearing protection that is not just functional but also expressive.; Customization options (e.g., color, logo) increase perceived value.; Direct-to-consumer sales can bypass traditional retail margins, allowing premium pricing.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a hearing protector with a unique design compared to a standard model.; Sales of limited-edition or personalized products will outpace standard models in a controlled test.; Direct-to-consumer sales will generate higher average order value than through retailers..

T2: Consumers will adopt differentiated hearing protection if it is marketed as a safety-first product that complies with stringent regulations, creating demand for trusted, reliable solutions. Who benefits: Safety-conscious consumers and industrial buyers who require certified, high-performance hearing protection.. Why behaviour changes: When a product is promoted as meeting or exceeding regulatory standards, consumers trust it more and are willing to pay a premium for assurance of safety and compliance.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by emphasizing certification, offering compliance-focused marketing, and selling through industrial channels where safety is paramount, potentially commanding higher margins.. Assumptions: Regulatory compliance is a primary purchase criterion for a significant segment of consumers.; Certification signals can be effectively communicated to end‑users.; Industrial buyers prioritize safety over price when selecting hearing protection.. Predictions: Surveyed industrial buyers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for a hearing protector with visible certification compared to a non‑certified model.; Sales of compliance‑focused products will be higher in regions with stringent safety regulations.; Partnerships with safety‑focused retailers will increase sales among industrial customers..

Homeownership of one-family detached homes rose significantly in the 1950s, modestly in the 1960s and 1970s, dropped slightly in the 1980s, and shows an extremely small increased in the 1990s, reaching 87 percent in 2000 (see graph).

An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.

International Harvester introduced the Cub Cadet in 1961; Wheel Horse, Bolens, and Simplicity, to mention a few, were also dominate players before John Deere came onto the scene.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.

Test "Creator Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 200 home-studio creators (YouTube, podcasting, live streaming) via creator forums and social media. Randomly assign participants to two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing high-quality audio and professional credibility (aligned with T1). Group B sees a product description emphasizing brand consistency across platforms and multi‑platform use (aligned with T2). Both groups view the same product price (e.g., €1,200). After viewing, participants indicate their likelihood to purchase (1–10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. The test measures the difference in purchase intent between the two product‑description frames.. Sample: 200 home-studio creators (100 per group). Measure: Purchase intent (1–10 scale) and maximum price willing to pay (euros).. Predictions: T1: Group A will report higher purchase intent and higher maximum price than Group B.; T2: Group B will report higher purchase intent and higher maximum price than Group A.. Decision rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Group A and Group B is at least 1.5 points on the 1‑10 scale, the theory that predicts the higher intent (T1 or T2) is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, neither theory is supported.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Comfort vs Fashion Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 300 adult consumers (150 per group) via a panel. Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing comfort and situational awareness (e.g., "engineered for hunters and shooting enthusiasts who demand superior reliability, situational awareness, and comfort"). Group B sees a product description emphasizing fashion and status (e.g., "stylish design, limited editions, premium pricing for fashion-conscious consumers"). Both groups view the same product image. After viewing, participants rate their intent to purchase on a 7-point Likert scale (1=Very unlikely, 7=Very likely).. Sample: 300 adult consumers (150 per group). Measure: Purchase intent (7-point Likert scale) for each group. Predictions: T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent than Group B because comfort and situational awareness are primary drivers.; T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent than Group A because fashion and status are primary drivers.. Decision rule: Calculate the average purchase intent for each group. If Group A’s average is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B’s average, conclude T1 is better supported. If Group B’s average is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A’s average, conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the evidence is inconclusive and the test is inconclusive.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

The test budget of €15,000 and 6‑week timeline are feasible within the given constraints. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

How value is captured: Jotun can charge a premium for a product that requires less maintenance, and capture market share by positioning itself as the high‑performance alternative.. Assumptions: Performance (durability, chip resistance) is a primary purchase criterion for marine coatings.; Jotun can demonstrate superior performance compared to competitors.; Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that requires less maintenance.. T1: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are affordable, practical for small gardens, and easy to maintain, creating a market demand that Deere can capture by offering a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Small‑holder homeowners and renters who need a versatile, inexpensive tool for yard work.. Why behaviour changes: Rising home ownership and small‑garden ownership increase the number of households seeking affordable, multipurpose yard equipment.. How value is captured: Deere can sell directly to consumers through its existing dealer network, offering a lower‑margin consumer product that leverages existing distribution and brand trust.. Assumptions: Small‑garden ownership and homeownership rates in 1962 are sufficient to create a sizable consumer market.; Consumers value affordability and ease of maintenance over premium features.; Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor at a price point that attracts individual buyers.. Predictions: Sales of lawn and garden tractors will grow faster than tractor sales to farms and large industrial users.; Deere will capture a share of the consumer market proportional to its dealer network coverage.; Consumer demand will be driven by price sensitivity and the need for a single tool for multiple yard tasks..

T2: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are a status symbol and a symbol of home ownership, creating a market demand that Deere can capture by offering a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes brand prestige. Why behaviour changes: Post‑World War II suburban growth and rising homeownership increase the number of households seeking products that signal affluence and community status.. How value is captured: Deere can price consumer tractors at a premium, leveraging its existing brand reputation and dealer network to sell directly to consumers, capturing higher margins.. Assumptions: Homeownership rates in 1962 are high enough to create a sizable market for status‑driven purchases.; Consumers associate Deere with quality and prestige, making it a desirable brand for status signaling.; Deere can produce a consumer‑grade tractor that maintains brand prestige while being affordable for middle‑income households.. Predictions: Sales of lawn and garden tractors will be concentrated in suburban and urban markets with high homeownership.; Deere will capture a share of the consumer market that is proportional to its brand prestige and dealer network presence.; Consumer demand will be driven by the desire to show off ownership and status rather than purely functional need..

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65 who own a small garden (under 1/4 acre). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a consumer‑grade lawn and garden tractor priced at $1,200 (approximately 1962‑era cost). Group B receives the same description but also emphasizes prestige and status signaling (e.g., "a tractor that shows your home’s value and your commitment to quality"). Both groups are told the tractor is available through a local dealer and can be financed. After reading the description, participants are asked: "Would you be interested in purchasing this tractor?" (binary response).. Sample: 500 homeowners (250 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who indicate "Yes" to purchasing).. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B because affordability and practicality are the primary drivers.; T2: Group B will have a purchase intent rate at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A because prestige and status signaling are the primary drivers.. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B, T1 is supported. If Group B’s purchase intent rate is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, neither theory is supported.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a stand-on body-fat analyser for home use because they value accurate body composition data for personal health tracking, and Tanita’s existing clinic/health club product demonstrates medical validity. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers seeking precise body fat measurement for weight management, fitness, or medical screening.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of body composition as a health indicator (e.g., Hiragana Times article) and medical evidence linking excess body fat to diseases (Tanita’s 1992 clinic launch) create demand for accurate, non-invasive measurement in. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by selling the analyser directly to consumers at retail or online, leveraging its existing brand trust and proven technology.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Tanita’s medical-grade accuracy from clinic use.; Retail distribution channels are accessible and cost-effective for a consumer product.; Price sensitivity is moderate for a health-focused device.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will express willingness to pay at least €150 for a home body-fat analyser.; Retail sales of a consumer version will exceed 5,000 units in the first year if positioned as a health-tracking tool..

T2: Consumers will adopt a stand-on body-fat analyser for home use because they value convenience and privacy, and Tanita’s existing clinic/health club product demonstrates a non-invasive, easy-to-use solution. Who benefits: Privacy-conscious consumers who prefer home testing over clinic visits, and those who value quick, non-intrusive health monitoring.. Why behaviour changes: Growing demand for at-home health monitoring (e.g., Hiragana Times article on household bathroom scales) and the convenience of a stand-on device without professional interaction create demand for a home version.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by offering a consumer version at retail or online, leveraging its existing brand trust and proven technology to differentiate from competitors.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize privacy and convenience over professional oversight.; Retail distribution channels are accessible and cost-effective for a consumer product.; Price sensitivity is moderate for a health-focused device.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will express willingness to pay at least €150 for a home body-fat analyser that can be used discreetly.; Retail sales of a consumer version will exceed 5,000 units in the first year if positioned as a convenient, private health tool..

Test "Consumer Willingness to Pay Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 500 Japanese adults aged 20-65 via a panel, stratified by gender and age. Randomly assign participants to one of two product descriptions: (A) a stand-on body-fat analyser marketed as a home health tool for personal tracking, emphasizing medical validity and accuracy; (B) the same analyser marketed as a convenient, private home test for those who value discretion, emphasizing ease of use and privacy. Both descriptions include price information (e.g., €150). After viewing the product. Sample: 500 Japanese adults (250 per group) recruited via an online panel, stratified by gender and age (20-35, 36-50, 51-65).. Measure: Primary outcome: maximum price participants would pay for the analyser (in euros). Secondary outcome: stated intent to purchase (binary: "Would buy" vs "Would not buy").. Predictions: T1: Group A will report a higher maximum price and higher intent to purchase than Group B because health-conscious consumers value medical validity and are willing to pay more for accurate body-fat data.; T2: Group B will report a higher maximum price and higher intent to purchase than Group A because privacy-conscious consumers value discretion and are willing to pay more for a home test that avoids clinic visits.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price in Group A exceeds the average maximum price in Group B by at least €20, conclude that T1 is better supported. If the opposite difference is observed, conclude that T2 is better supported. If the difference is ≤€20, conclude that neither. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Home-Studio Creator Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 300 home-studio creators (defined as individuals who use microphones for personal content creation, not professionals). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing professional-grade audio quality and brand reputation; Group B sees a product description emphasizing premium brand prestige and prestige-driven pricing. Both groups view the same product (a mid-range Neumann microphone) and are asked: "Would you purchase this microphone for your home studio?" (binary yes/no).. Sample: 300 home-studio creators recruited via social media and creator forums, balanced for gender, age, and experience.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary yes/no) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent than Group B because creators prioritize professional-grade audio quality.; T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent than Group A because creators value brand prestige and are willing to pay a premium for prestige.. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B’s, conclude T1 is better supported. If Group B’s purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A’s, conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.
